<h1 class="epydoc">Source Code for <a href="RDFClosure-module.html">Package RDFClosure</a></h1>
<pre class="py-src">
<a name="L1"></a><tt class="py-lineno">  1</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-comment"># -*- coding: utf-8 -*-</tt> </tt>
<a name="L2"></a><tt class="py-lineno">  2</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-comment">#</tt> </tt>
<a name="L3"></a><tt class="py-lineno">  3</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring">"""</tt> </tt>
<a name="L4"></a><tt class="py-lineno">  4</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring">This module is brute force implementation of the 'finite' version of U{RDFS semantics&lt;http://www.w3.org/TR/rdf-mt/&gt;}</tt> </tt>
<a name="L5"></a><tt class="py-lineno">  5</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring">and of U{OWL 2 RL&lt;http://www.w3.org/TR/owl2-profiles/#Reasoning_in_OWL_2_RL_and_RDF_Graphs_using_Rules&gt;}</tt> </tt>
<a name="L6"></a><tt class="py-lineno">  6</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring">on the top of RDFLib (with some caveats, see below). Some extensions to these are also implemented.</tt> </tt>
<a name="L7"></a><tt class="py-lineno">  7</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring">Brute force means that, in all cases, simple forward chaining rules are used to extend (recursively) the incoming graph with all triples</tt> </tt>
<a name="L8"></a><tt class="py-lineno">  8</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring">that the rule sets permit (ie, the "deductive closure" of the graph is computed).</tt> </tt>
<a name="L9"></a><tt class="py-lineno">  9</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring">There is an extra options whether the axiomatic triples are added to the graph (prior to the forward chaining step).</tt> </tt>
<a name="L10"></a><tt class="py-lineno"> 10</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring">These, typically set the domain and range for properties or define some core classes.</tt> </tt>
<a name="L11"></a><tt class="py-lineno"> 11</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring">In the case of RDFS, the implementation uses a 'finite' version of the axiomatic triples only (as proposed, for example,</tt> </tt>
<a name="L12"></a><tt class="py-lineno"> 12</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring">by Herman ter Horst). This means that it adds only those C{rdf:_i} type predicates that do appear in the original graph,</tt> </tt>
<a name="L13"></a><tt class="py-lineno"> 13</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring">thereby keeping this step finite. For OWL 2 RL, OWL 2 does not define axiomatic triples formally; but they can be deduced from the</tt> </tt>
<a name="L14"></a><tt class="py-lineno"> 14</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring">U{OWL 2 RDF Based Semantics&lt;http://www.w3.org/TR/owl2-rdf-based-semantics/&gt;} document and are listed in Appendix 6 (though informally).</tt> </tt>
<a name="L15"></a><tt class="py-lineno"> 15</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring">Note, however, that this implementation adds only those triples that refer to OWL terms that are meaningful for the OWL 2 RL case.</tt> </tt>
<a name="L16"></a><tt class="py-lineno"> 16</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring"></tt> </tt>
<a name="L17"></a><tt class="py-lineno"> 17</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring"></tt> </tt>
<a name="L18"></a><tt class="py-lineno"> 18</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring">Package Entry Points</tt> </tt>
<a name="L19"></a><tt class="py-lineno"> 19</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring">====================</tt> </tt>
<a name="L20"></a><tt class="py-lineno"> 20</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring"></tt> </tt>
<a name="L21"></a><tt class="py-lineno"> 21</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring">The main entry point to the package is via the L{DeductiveClosure&lt;DeductiveClosure&gt;} class. This class should be initialized to control</tt> </tt>
<a name="L22"></a><tt class="py-lineno"> 22</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring">the parameters of the deductive closure; the forward chaining is done via the L{expand&lt;DeductiveClosure.expand&gt;} method.</tt> </tt>
<a name="L23"></a><tt class="py-lineno"> 23</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring">The simplest way to use the package from an RDFLib application is as follows::</tt> </tt>
<a name="L24"></a><tt class="py-lineno"> 24</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring"></tt> </tt>
<a name="L25"></a><tt class="py-lineno"> 25</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring">        graph = Graph()                                 # creation of an RDFLib graph</tt> </tt>
<a name="L26"></a><tt class="py-lineno"> 26</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring">        ...</tt> </tt>
<a name="L27"></a><tt class="py-lineno"> 27</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring">        ...                                             # normal RDFLib application, eg, parsing RDF data</tt> </tt>
<a name="L28"></a><tt class="py-lineno"> 28</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring">        ...</tt> </tt>
<a name="L29"></a><tt class="py-lineno"> 29</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring">        DeductiveClosure(OWLRL_Semantics).expand(graph) # calculate an OWL 2 RL deductive closure of graph</tt> </tt>
<a name="L30"></a><tt class="py-lineno"> 30</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring">                                                        # without axiomatic triples</tt> </tt>
<a name="L31"></a><tt class="py-lineno"> 31</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring"></tt> </tt>
<a name="L32"></a><tt class="py-lineno"> 32</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring">The first argument of the C{DeductiveClosure} initialization can be replaced by other classes, providing different</tt> </tt>
<a name="L33"></a><tt class="py-lineno"> 33</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring">types of deductive closure; other arguments are also possible. For example::</tt> </tt>
<a name="L34"></a><tt class="py-lineno"> 34</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring"></tt> </tt>
<a name="L35"></a><tt class="py-lineno"> 35</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring"> DeductiveClosure(OWLRL_Extension, rdfs_closure = True, axiomatic_triples = True, datatype_axioms = True).expand(graph)</tt> </tt>
<a name="L36"></a><tt class="py-lineno"> 36</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring"></tt> </tt>
<a name="L37"></a><tt class="py-lineno"> 37</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring">will calculate the deductive closure including RDFS and some extensions to OWL 2 RL, and with all possible axiomatic</tt> </tt>
<a name="L38"></a><tt class="py-lineno"> 38</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring">triples added to the graph (this is about the maximum the package can do&#8230;)</tt> </tt>
<a name="L39"></a><tt class="py-lineno"> 39</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring"></tt> </tt>
<a name="L40"></a><tt class="py-lineno"> 40</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring">The same instance of L{DeductiveClosure&lt;DeductiveClosure&gt;} can be used for several graph expansions. In other words, the expand function does not change any state.</tt> </tt>
<a name="L41"></a><tt class="py-lineno"> 41</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring"></tt> </tt>
<a name="L42"></a><tt class="py-lineno"> 42</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring">For convenience, a second entry point to the package is provided in the form of a function called L{convert_graph&lt;convert_graph&gt;},</tt> </tt>
<a name="L43"></a><tt class="py-lineno"> 43</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring">that expects a directory with various options, including a file name. The function parses the file, creates the expanded graph, and serializes the result into RDF/XML or</tt> </tt>
<a name="L44"></a><tt class="py-lineno"> 44</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring">Turtle. This function is particularly useful as an entry point for a CGI call (where the HTML form parameters are in a directory) and</tt> </tt>
<a name="L45"></a><tt class="py-lineno"> 45</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring">is easy to use with a command line interface. The package distribution contains an example for both.</tt> </tt>
<a name="L46"></a><tt class="py-lineno"> 46</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring"></tt> </tt>
<a name="L47"></a><tt class="py-lineno"> 47</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring">There are major closure type (ie, semantic closure possibilities); these can be controlled through the appropriate</tt> </tt>
<a name="L48"></a><tt class="py-lineno"> 48</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring">parameters of the L{DeductiveClosure&lt;DeductiveClosure&gt;} class:</tt> </tt>
<a name="L49"></a><tt class="py-lineno"> 49</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring"></tt> </tt>
<a name="L50"></a><tt class="py-lineno"> 50</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring">        - using the L{RDFS_Semantics&lt;RDFSClosure.RDFS_Semantics&gt;} class, implementing the U{RDFS semantics&lt;http://www.w3.org/TR/rdf-mt/&gt;}</tt> </tt>
<a name="L51"></a><tt class="py-lineno"> 51</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring">        - using the L{OWLRL_Semantics&lt;OWLRL.OWLRL_Semantics&gt;} class, implementing the U{OWL 2 RL&lt;http://www.w3.org/TR/owl2-profiles/#Reasoning_in_OWL_2_RL_and_RDF_Graphs_using_Rules&gt;}</tt> </tt>
<a name="L52"></a><tt class="py-lineno"> 52</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring">        - using L{RDFS_OWLRL_Semantics&lt;CombinedClosure.RDFS_OWLRL_Semantics&gt;} class, implementing a combined semantics of U{RDFS semantics&lt;http://www.w3.org/TR/rdf-mt/&gt;} and U{OWL 2 RL&lt;http://www.w3.org/TR/owl2-profiles/#Reasoning_in_OWL_2_RL_and_RDF_Graphs_using_Rules&gt;}</tt> </tt>
<a name="L53"></a><tt class="py-lineno"> 53</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring"></tt> </tt>
<a name="L54"></a><tt class="py-lineno"> 54</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring">In all three cases there are other dimensions that can control the exact closure being generated:</tt> </tt>
<a name="L55"></a><tt class="py-lineno"> 55</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring"></tt> </tt>
<a name="L56"></a><tt class="py-lineno"> 56</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring"> - for convenience, the so called axiomatic triples (see, eg, the U{axiomatic triples in RDFS&lt;http://www.w3.org/TR/rdf-mt/#rdfs_interp&gt;}) are, by default, I{not} added to the graph closure to reduce the number of generated triples. These can be controlled through a separate initialization argument</tt> </tt>
<a name="L57"></a><tt class="py-lineno"> 57</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring"> - similarly, the axiomatic triples for D-entailment are separated</tt> </tt>
<a name="L58"></a><tt class="py-lineno"> 58</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring"></tt> </tt>
<a name="L59"></a><tt class="py-lineno"> 59</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring">Some Technical/implementation aspects</tt> </tt>
<a name="L60"></a><tt class="py-lineno"> 60</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring">=====================================</tt> </tt>
<a name="L61"></a><tt class="py-lineno"> 61</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring"></tt> </tt>
<a name="L62"></a><tt class="py-lineno"> 62</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring">The core processing is done in the in the L{Core&lt;Closure.Core&gt;} class, which is subclassed by the L{RDFS&lt;RDFS_Semantics&gt;} and</tt> </tt>
<a name="L63"></a><tt class="py-lineno"> 63</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring">the L{OWL 2 RL&lt;OWLRL_Semantics&gt;} classes (these two are then, on their turn, subclassed by the</tt> </tt>
<a name="L64"></a><tt class="py-lineno"> 64</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring">L{RDFS + OWL 2 RL Semantics&lt;CombinedClosure.RDFS_OWLRL_Semantics&gt;}) class). The core implements the core functionality of cycling</tt> </tt>
<a name="L65"></a><tt class="py-lineno"> 65</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring">through the rules, whereas the rules themselves are defined and implemented in the subclasses. There are also methods that are executed only once either</tt> </tt>
<a name="L66"></a><tt class="py-lineno"> 66</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring">at the beginning or at the end of the full processing cycle. Adding axiomatic triples is handled separately, which allows a finer user control over</tt> </tt>
<a name="L67"></a><tt class="py-lineno"> 67</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring">these features.</tt> </tt>
<a name="L68"></a><tt class="py-lineno"> 68</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring"></tt> </tt>
<a name="L69"></a><tt class="py-lineno"> 69</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring">Literals must be handled separately. Indeed, the functionality relies on 'extended' RDF graphs, that allows literals</tt> </tt>
<a name="L70"></a><tt class="py-lineno"> 70</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring">to be in a subject position, too. Because RDFLib does not allow that, processing begins by exchanging all literals in the</tt> </tt>
<a name="L71"></a><tt class="py-lineno"> 71</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring">graph for bnodes (identical literals get the same associated bnode). Processing occurs on these bnodes; at the end of the process</tt> </tt>
<a name="L72"></a><tt class="py-lineno"> 72</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring">all these bnodes are replaced by their corresponding literals if possible (if the bnode occurs in a subject position, that triple</tt> </tt>
<a name="L73"></a><tt class="py-lineno"> 73</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring">is removed from the resulting graph). Details of this processing is handled in the separate L{Literals Proxies&lt;RDFClosure.Literals.LiteralProxies&gt;}</tt> </tt>
<a name="L74"></a><tt class="py-lineno"> 74</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring">class.</tt> </tt>
<a name="L75"></a><tt class="py-lineno"> 75</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring"></tt> </tt>
<a name="L76"></a><tt class="py-lineno"> 76</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring">The OWL specification includes references to datatypes that are not in the core RDFS specification, consequently not</tt> </tt>
<a name="L77"></a><tt class="py-lineno"> 77</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring">directly implemented by RDFLib. These are added in a separate module of the package.</tt> </tt>
<a name="L78"></a><tt class="py-lineno"> 78</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring"></tt> </tt>
<a name="L79"></a><tt class="py-lineno"> 79</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring"></tt> </tt>
<a name="L80"></a><tt class="py-lineno"> 80</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring">Problems with Literals with datatypes</tt> </tt>
<a name="L81"></a><tt class="py-lineno"> 81</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring">-------------------------------------</tt> </tt>
<a name="L82"></a><tt class="py-lineno"> 82</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring"></tt> </tt>
<a name="L83"></a><tt class="py-lineno"> 83</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring">The current distribution of RDFLib is fairly poor in handling datatypes, particularly in checking whether a lexical form</tt> </tt>
<a name="L84"></a><tt class="py-lineno"> 84</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring">of a literal is "proper" as for its declared datatype. A typical example is::</tt> </tt>
<a name="L85"></a><tt class="py-lineno"> 85</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring">  "-1234"^^xsd:nonNegativeInteger</tt> </tt>
<a name="L86"></a><tt class="py-lineno"> 86</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring">which should not be accepted as valid literal. Because the requirements of OWL 2 RL are much stricter in this respect, an alternative set of datatype handling (essentially, conversions) had to be implemented (see the L{XsdDatatypes} module).</tt> </tt>
<a name="L87"></a><tt class="py-lineno"> 87</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring"></tt> </tt>
<a name="L88"></a><tt class="py-lineno"> 88</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring">The L{DeductiveClosure&lt;DeductiveClosure&gt;} class has an additional instance variable whether</tt> </tt>
<a name="L89"></a><tt class="py-lineno"> 89</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring">the default RDFLib conversion routines should be exchanged against the new ones. If this flag is set to True and instance creation (this is</tt> </tt>
<a name="L90"></a><tt class="py-lineno"> 90</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring">the default), then the conversion routines are set back</tt> </tt>
<a name="L91"></a><tt class="py-lineno"> 91</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring">to the originals once the expansion is complete, thereby avoiding to influence older application that may not work properly with the</tt> </tt>
<a name="L92"></a><tt class="py-lineno"> 92</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring">new set of conversion routines.</tt> </tt>
<a name="L93"></a><tt class="py-lineno"> 93</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring"></tt> </tt>
<a name="L94"></a><tt class="py-lineno"> 94</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring">If the user wants to use these alternative lexical conversions everywhere in the application, then</tt> </tt>
<a name="L95"></a><tt class="py-lineno"> 95</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring">the L{use_improved_datatypes_conversions&lt;DeductiveClosure.use_improved_datatypes_conversions&gt;} method can be invoked. That method changes</tt> </tt>
<a name="L96"></a><tt class="py-lineno"> 96</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring">the conversion routines and, from that point on, all usage of L{DeductiveClosure&lt;DeductiveClosure&gt;} instances will use the</tt> </tt>
<a name="L97"></a><tt class="py-lineno"> 97</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring">improved conversion methods without resetting them. Ie, the code structure can be something like::</tt> </tt>
<a name="L98"></a><tt class="py-lineno"> 98</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring">  DeductiveClosure().use_improved_datatypes_conversions()</tt> </tt>
<a name="L99"></a><tt class="py-lineno"> 99</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring">  ... RDFLib application</tt> </tt>
<a name="L100"></a><tt class="py-lineno">100</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring">  DeductiveClosure().expand(graph)</tt> </tt>
<a name="L101"></a><tt class="py-lineno">101</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring">  ...</tt> </tt>
<a name="L102"></a><tt class="py-lineno">102</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring">The default situation can be set back using the L{use_rdflib_datatypes_conversions&lt;DeductiveClosure.use_improved_datatypes_conversions&gt;} call.</tt> </tt>
<a name="L103"></a><tt class="py-lineno">103</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring"></tt> </tt>
<a name="L104"></a><tt class="py-lineno">104</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring">It is, however, not I{required} to use these methods at all. Ie, the user can use::</tt> </tt>
<a name="L105"></a><tt class="py-lineno">105</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring">  DeductiveClosure(improved_datatypes=False).expand(graph)</tt> </tt>
<a name="L106"></a><tt class="py-lineno">106</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring">which will result in a proper graph expansion except for the datatype specific comparisons which will be incomplete.</tt> </tt>
<a name="L107"></a><tt class="py-lineno">107</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring"></tt> </tt>
<a name="L108"></a><tt class="py-lineno">108</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring"></tt> </tt>
<a name="L109"></a><tt class="py-lineno">109</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring"></tt> </tt>
<a name="L110"></a><tt class="py-lineno">110</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring">Problems with Literals with datatypes</tt> </tt>
<a name="L111"></a><tt class="py-lineno">111</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring">-------------------------------------</tt> </tt>
<a name="L112"></a><tt class="py-lineno">112</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring"></tt> </tt>
<a name="L113"></a><tt class="py-lineno">113</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring">The current distribution of RDFLib is fairly poor in handling datatypes, particularly in checking whether a lexical form</tt> </tt>
<a name="L114"></a><tt class="py-lineno">114</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring">of a literal is "proper" as for its declared datatype. A typical example is::</tt> </tt>
<a name="L115"></a><tt class="py-lineno">115</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring">  "-1234"^^xsd:nonNegativeInteger</tt> </tt>
<a name="L116"></a><tt class="py-lineno">116</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring">which should not be accepted as valid literal. Because the requirements of OWL 2 RL are much stricter in this respect, an alternative set of datatype handling (essentially, conversions) had to be implemented (see the L{XsdDatatypes} module).</tt> </tt>
<a name="L117"></a><tt class="py-lineno">117</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring"></tt> </tt>
<a name="L118"></a><tt class="py-lineno">118</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring">The L{DeductiveClosure&lt;DeductiveClosure&gt;} class has an additional instance variable whether</tt> </tt>
<a name="L119"></a><tt class="py-lineno">119</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring">the default RDFLib conversion routines should be exchanged against the new ones. If this flag is set to True and instance creation (this is</tt> </tt>
<a name="L120"></a><tt class="py-lineno">120</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring">the default), then the conversion routines are set back</tt> </tt>
<a name="L121"></a><tt class="py-lineno">121</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring">to the originals once the expansion is complete, thereby avoiding to influence older application that may not work properly with the</tt> </tt>
<a name="L122"></a><tt class="py-lineno">122</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring">new set of conversion routines.</tt> </tt>
<a name="L123"></a><tt class="py-lineno">123</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring"></tt> </tt>
<a name="L124"></a><tt class="py-lineno">124</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring">If the user wants to use these alternative lexical conversions everywhere in the application, then</tt> </tt>
<a name="L125"></a><tt class="py-lineno">125</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring">the L{use_improved_datatypes_conversions&lt;DeductiveClosure.use_improved_datatypes_conversions&gt;} method can be invoked. That method changes</tt> </tt>
<a name="L126"></a><tt class="py-lineno">126</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring">the conversion routines and, from that point on, all usage of L{DeductiveClosure&lt;DeductiveClosure&gt;} instances will use the</tt> </tt>
<a name="L127"></a><tt class="py-lineno">127</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring">improved conversion methods without resetting them. Ie, the code structure can be something like::</tt> </tt>
<a name="L128"></a><tt class="py-lineno">128</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring">  DeductiveClosure().use_improved_datatypes_conversions()</tt> </tt>
<a name="L129"></a><tt class="py-lineno">129</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring">  ... RDFLib application</tt> </tt>
<a name="L130"></a><tt class="py-lineno">130</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring">  DeductiveClosure().expand(graph)</tt> </tt>
<a name="L131"></a><tt class="py-lineno">131</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring">  ...</tt> </tt>
<a name="L132"></a><tt class="py-lineno">132</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring">The default situation can be set back using the L{use_rdflib_datatypes_conversions&lt;DeductiveClosure.use_improved_datatypes_conversions&gt;} call.</tt> </tt>
<a name="L133"></a><tt class="py-lineno">133</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring"></tt> </tt>
<a name="L134"></a><tt class="py-lineno">134</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring">It is, however, not I{required} to use these methods at all. Ie, the user can use::</tt> </tt>
<a name="L135"></a><tt class="py-lineno">135</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring">  DeductiveClosure(improved_datatypes=False).expand(graph)</tt> </tt>
<a name="L136"></a><tt class="py-lineno">136</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring">which will result in a proper graph expansion except for the datatype specific comparisons which will be incomplete.</tt> </tt>
<a name="L137"></a><tt class="py-lineno">137</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring"></tt> </tt>
<a name="L138"></a><tt class="py-lineno">138</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring"></tt> </tt>

<a name="L198"></a><tt class="py-lineno">198</tt> <a class="py-toggle" href="#" id="__parse_input-toggle" onclick="return toggle('__parse_input');">-</a><tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-keyword">def</tt> <a class="py-def-name" href="RDFClosure-module.html#__parse_input">__parse_input</a><tt class="py-op">(</tt><tt class="py-param">iformat</tt><tt class="py-op">,</tt> <tt class="py-param">inp</tt><tt class="py-op">,</tt> <tt class="py-param">graph</tt><tt class="py-op">)</tt><tt class="py-op">:</tt> </tt>
</div><div id="__parse_input-collapsed" style="display:none;" pad="+++" indent="++++"></div><div id="__parse_input-expanded"><a name="L199"></a><tt class="py-lineno">199</tt>  <tt class="py-line">        <tt class="py-docstring">"""Parse the input into the graph, possibly checking the suffix for the format.</tt> </tt>
<a name="L200"></a><tt class="py-lineno">200</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring">        </tt> </tt>
<a name="L201"></a><tt class="py-lineno">201</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring">        @param iformat: input format; can be one of L{AUTO}, L{TURTLE}, or L{RDFXML}. L{AUTO} means that the suffix of the file name or URI will decide: '.ttl' means Turtle, RDF/XML otherwise.</tt> </tt>
<a name="L202"></a><tt class="py-lineno">202</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring">        @param inp: input file; anything that RDFLib accepts in that position (URI, file name, file object). If '-', standard input is used.</tt> </tt>
<a name="L203"></a><tt class="py-lineno">203</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring">        @param graph: the RDFLib Graph instance to parse into.  </tt> </tt>
<a name="L204"></a><tt class="py-lineno">204</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring">        """</tt> </tt>
<a name="L205"></a><tt class="py-lineno">205</tt>  <tt class="py-line">        <tt class="py-keyword">if</tt> <tt class="py-name">iformat</tt> <tt class="py-op">==</tt> <tt id="link-28" class="py-name"><a title="RDFClosure.AUTO" class="py-name" href="#" onclick="return doclink('link-28', 'AUTO', 'link-19');">AUTO</a></tt><tt class="py-op">:</tt> </tt>
<a name="L206"></a><tt class="py-lineno">206</tt>  <tt class="py-line">                <tt class="py-keyword">if</tt> <tt class="py-name">inp</tt> <tt class="py-op">==</tt> <tt class="py-string">"-"</tt><tt class="py-op">:</tt> </tt>

<a name="L385"></a><tt class="py-lineno">385</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring">        and serialize back the result in some format.</tt> </tt>
<a name="L386"></a><tt class="py-lineno">386</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring">        Note that this entry point can be used requiring no entailment at all;</tt> </tt>
<a name="L387"></a><tt class="py-lineno">387</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring">        because both the input and the output format for the package can be RDF/XML or Turtle, such usage would</tt> </tt>
<a name="L388"></a><tt class="py-lineno">388</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring">        simply mean a format conversion.</tt> </tt>

<a name="L390"></a><tt class="py-lineno">390</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring">        If OWL 2 RL processing is required, that also means that the owl:imports statements are interpreted. Ie,</tt> </tt>
<a name="L391"></a><tt class="py-lineno">391</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring">        ontologies can be spread over several files. Note, however, that the output of the process would then include all </tt> </tt>
<a name="L392"></a><tt class="py-lineno">392</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring">        imported ontologies, too.</tt> </tt>

<a name="L394"></a><tt class="py-lineno">394</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring">        @param options: object with specific attributes, namely:</tt> </tt>
<a name="L395"></a><tt class="py-lineno">395</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring">          - options.sources: list of uris or file names for the source data; for each one if the name ends with 'ttl', it is considered to be turtle, RDF/XML otherwise (this can be overwritten by the options.iformat, though)</tt> </tt>
<a name="L396"></a><tt class="py-lineno">396</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring">          - options.text: direct Turtle encoding of a graph as a text string (useful, eg, for a CGI call using a text field)</tt> </tt>

<a name="L399"></a><tt class="py-lineno">399</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring">          - options.owlExtras: can be yes or no; whether the extra rules beyond OWL 2 RL are used or not.</tt> </tt>
<a name="L400"></a><tt class="py-lineno">400</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring">          - options.axioms: whether relevant axiomatic triples are added before chaining (can be a boolean, or the strings "yes" or "no")</tt> </tt>
<a name="L401"></a><tt class="py-lineno">401</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring">          - options.daxioms: further datatype axiomatic triples are added to the output (can be a boolean, or the strings "yes" or "no")</tt> </tt>
<a name="L402"></a><tt class="py-lineno">402</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring">          - options.format: output format, can be "turtle" or "rdfxml"</tt> </tt>
<a name="L403"></a><tt class="py-lineno">403</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring">          - options.iformat: input format, can be "turtle", "rdfa", "json", "rdfxml", or "auto". "auto" means that the suffix of the file is considered: '.ttl'. '.html', 'json' or '.jsonld' respectively with 'xml' as a fallback</tt> </tt>
<a name="L404"></a><tt class="py-lineno">404</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring">          - options.trimming: whether the extension to OWLRL should also include trimming</tt> </tt>
<a name="L405"></a><tt class="py-lineno">405</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring">        @param closureClass: explicit class reference. If set, this overrides the various different other options to be used as an extension.</tt> </tt>

<h1 class="epydoc">Module Closure</h1><p class="nomargin-top"><span class="codelink"><a href="RDFClosure.Closure-pysrc.html">source&nbsp;code</a></span></p>
<p>The generic superclasses for various rule based semantics and the 
  possible extensions.</p>

<a name="Core.store_triple"></a><div id="Core.store_triple-def"><a name="L180"></a><tt class="py-lineno">180</tt> <a class="py-toggle" href="#" id="Core.store_triple-toggle" onclick="return toggle('Core.store_triple');">-</a><tt class="py-line">        <tt class="py-keyword">def</tt> <a class="py-def-name" href="RDFClosure.Closure.Core-class.html#store_triple">store_triple</a><tt class="py-op">(</tt><tt class="py-param">self</tt><tt class="py-op">,</tt> <tt class="py-param">t</tt><tt class="py-op">)</tt><tt class="py-op">:</tt> </tt>
</div><div id="Core.store_triple-collapsed" style="display:none;" pad="+++" indent="++++++++++++"></div><div id="Core.store_triple-expanded"><a name="L181"></a><tt class="py-lineno">181</tt>  <tt class="py-line">                <tt class="py-docstring">"""</tt> </tt>
<a name="L182"></a><tt class="py-lineno">182</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring">                In contrast to its name, this does not yet add anything to the graph itself, it just stores the tuple in an</tt> </tt>
<a name="L183"></a><tt class="py-lineno">183</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring">                L{internal set&lt;Core.added_triples&gt;}. (It is important for this to be a set: some of the rules in the various closures may</tt> </tt>
<a name="L184"></a><tt class="py-lineno">184</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring">                generate the same tuples several times.) Before adding the tuple to the set, the method checks whether</tt> </tt>
<a name="L185"></a><tt class="py-lineno">185</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring">                the tuple is in the final graph already (if yes, it is not added to the set).</tt> </tt>
<a name="L186"></a><tt class="py-lineno">186</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring"></tt> </tt>
<a name="L187"></a><tt class="py-lineno">187</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring">                The set itself is emptied at the start of every processing cycle; the triples are then effectively added to the</tt> </tt>
<a name="L188"></a><tt class="py-lineno">188</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring">                graph at the end of such a cycle. If the set is</tt> </tt>
<a name="L189"></a><tt class="py-lineno">189</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring">                actually empty at that point, this means that the cycle has not added any new triple, and the full processing can stop.</tt> </tt>
<a name="L190"></a><tt class="py-lineno">190</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring"></tt> </tt>
<a name="L191"></a><tt class="py-lineno">191</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring">                @param t: the triple to be added to the graph, unless it is already there</tt> </tt>

<!-- ==================== CLASS DESCRIPTION ==================== -->
<h1 class="epydoc">Class Core</h1><p class="nomargin-top"><span class="codelink"><a href="RDFClosure.Closure-pysrc.html#Core">source&nbsp;code</a></span></p>
<dl><dt>Known Subclasses:</dt>
<dd>
      <ul class="subclass-list">
<li><a href="RDFClosure.RDFSClosure.RDFS_Semantics-class.html">RDFSClosure.RDFS_Semantics</a></li><li>, <a href="RDFClosure.OWLRL.OWLRL_Semantics-class.html">OWLRL.OWLRL_Semantics</a></li>  </ul>
</dd></dl>

<hr />
<p>Core of the semantics management, dealing with the RDFS and other 
  Semantic triples. The only reason to have it in a separate class is for 
  an easier maintainability.</p>
  <p>This is a common superclass only. In the present module, it is 
  subclassed by a <a 
  href="RDFClosure.RDFSClosure.RDFS_Semantics-class.html" class="link">RDFS
  Closure</a> class and a <a 
  href="RDFClosure.OWLRL.OWLRL_Semantics-class.html" class="link">OWL RL 
  Closure</a> classes. There are some methods that are implemented in the 
  subclasses only, ie, this class cannot be used by itself!</p>

<div>

  but before handling possible errors (ie, the method can add its own error
  messages). By default, this method is empty, subclasses can add content 
  to it by overriding it.</p>

<a name="rules"></a>
<div>
<table class="details" border="1" cellpadding="3"
       cellspacing="0" width="100%" bgcolor="white">
<tr><td>
  <table width="100%" cellpadding="0" cellspacing="0" border="0">
  <tr valign="top"><td>
  <h3 class="epydoc"><span class="sig"><span class="sig-name">rules</span>(<span class="sig-arg">self</span>,
        <span class="sig-arg">t</span>,
        <span class="sig-arg">cycle_num</span>)</span>
  </h3>
  </td><td align="right" valign="top"
    ><span class="codelink"><a href="RDFClosure.Closure-pysrc.html#Core.rules">source&nbsp;code</a></span>&nbsp;
    </td>
  </tr></table>
  
  <p>The core processing cycles through every tuple in the graph and 
  dispatches it to the various methods implementing a specific group of 
  rules. By default, this method raises an exception; indeed, subclasses 
  <i>must</i> add content to by overriding it.</p>
  <dl class="fields">
    <dt>Parameters:</dt>
    <dd><ul class="nomargin-top">
        <li><strong class="pname"><code>t</code></strong> (tuple) - one triple on which to apply the rules</li>
        <li><strong class="pname"><code>cycle_num</code></strong> - which cycle are we in, starting with 1. This value is forwarded 
          to all local rules; it is also used locally to collect the bnodes
          in the graph.</li>
    </ul></dd>
  </dl>
</td></tr></table>
</div>

<a name="store_triple"></a>
<div>
<table class="details" border="1" cellpadding="3"
       cellspacing="0" width="100%" bgcolor="white">
<tr><td>
  <table width="100%" cellpadding="0" cellspacing="0" border="0">
  <tr valign="top"><td>
  <h3 class="epydoc"><span class="sig"><span class="sig-name">store_triple</span>(<span class="sig-arg">self</span>,
        <span class="sig-arg">t</span>)</span>
  </h3>
  </td><td align="right" valign="top"
    ><span class="codelink"><a href="RDFClosure.Closure-pysrc.html#Core.store_triple">source&nbsp;code</a></span>&nbsp;
    </td>
  </tr></table>
  
  <p>In contrast to its name, this does not yet add anything to the graph 
  itself, it just stores the tuple in an <a 
  href="RDFClosure.Closure.Core-class.html#added_triples" 
  class="link">internal set</a>. (It is important for this to be a set: 
  some of the rules in the various closures may generate the same tuples 
  several times.) Before adding the tuple to the set, the method checks 
  whether the tuple is in the final graph already (if yes, it is not added 
  to the set).</p>
  <p>The set itself is emptied at the start of every processing cycle; the 
  triples are then effectively added to the graph at the end of such a 
  cycle. If the set is actually empty at that point, this means that the 
  cycle has not added any new triple, and the full processing can stop.</p>
  <dl class="fields">
    <dt>Parameters:</dt>
    <dd><ul class="nomargin-top">
        <li><strong class="pname"><code>t</code></strong> (a 3-element tuple of (s,p,o)) - the triple to be added to the graph, unless it is already there</li>
    </ul></dd>
  </dl>
</td></tr></table>
</div>
<a name="closure"></a>
<div>
<table class="details" border="1" cellpadding="3"
       cellspacing="0" width="100%" bgcolor="white">
<tr><td>
  <table width="100%" cellpadding="0" cellspacing="0" border="0">
  <tr valign="top"><td>
  <h3 class="epydoc"><span class="sig"><span class="sig-name">closure</span>(<span class="sig-arg">self</span>)</span>
  </h3>
  </td><td align="right" valign="top"
    ><span class="codelink"><a href="RDFClosure.Closure-pysrc.html#Core.closure">source&nbsp;code</a></span>&nbsp;
    </td>
  </tr></table>
  
  <p>Generate the closure the graph. This is the real 'core'.</p>
  <p>The processing rules store new triples via the <a 
  href="RDFClosure.Closure.Core-class.html#store_triple" 
  class="link">separate method</a> which stores them in the <a 
  href="RDFClosure.Closure.Core-class.html#added_triples" 
  class="link">added_triples</a> array. If that array is emtpy at the end 
  of a cycle, it means that the whole process can be stopped.</p>
  <p>If required, the relevant axiomatic triples are added to the graph 
  before processing in cycles. Similarly the exchange of literals against 
  bnodes is also done in this step (and restored after all cycles are 
  over).</p>
  <dl class="fields">
  </dl>
</td></tr></table>
</div>

<!-- ==================== MODULE DESCRIPTION ==================== -->
<h1 class="epydoc">Module CombinedClosure</h1><p class="nomargin-top"><span class="codelink"><a href="RDFClosure.CombinedClosure-pysrc.html">source&nbsp;code</a></span></p>
<p>The combined closure: performing <i>both</i> the OWL 2 RL and RDFS 
  closures. The two are very close but there are some rules in RDFS that 
  are not in OWL 2 RL (eg, the axiomatic triples concerning the container 
  membership properties). Using this closure class the OWL 2 RL 
  implementation becomes a full extension of RDFS.</p>

<hr />
<div class="fields">      <p><strong>Requires:</strong>
        <a href="https://github.com/RDFLib/rdflib" 
        target="_top">RDFLib</a>, 4.0.0 and higher
      </p>
      <p><strong>License:</strong>
        This software is available for use under the <a 
        href="http://www.w3.org/Consortium/Legal/2002/copyright-software-20021231"
        target="_top">W3C Software License</a>
      </p>
      <p><strong>Organization:</strong>
        <a href="http://www.w3.org" target="_top">World Wide Web 
        Consortium</a>
      </p>
      <p><strong>Author:</strong>
        <a href="http://ahref=&quot;http://www.w3.org/People/Ivan/&quot;" 
        target="_top">Ivan Herman</a>
      </p>
      <p><strong>Contact:</strong>
        Ivan Herman, ivan@w3.org
      </p>
</div><!-- ==================== CLASSES ==================== -->

<a name="RDFS_OWLRL_Semantics"></a><div id="RDFS_OWLRL_Semantics-def"><a name="L26"></a><tt class="py-lineno"> 26</tt>  <tt class="py-line"> </tt>
<a name="L27"></a><tt class="py-lineno"> 27</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-comment">######################################################################################################</tt> </tt>
<a name="L28"></a><tt class="py-lineno"> 28</tt>  <tt class="py-line"> </tt>
<a name="L29"></a><tt class="py-lineno"> 29</tt>  <tt class="py-line"> </tt>
<a name="L30"></a><tt class="py-lineno"> 30</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-comment"># noinspection PyPep8Naming</tt> </tt>
<a name="L31"></a><tt class="py-lineno"> 31</tt> <a class="py-toggle" href="#" id="RDFS_OWLRL_Semantics-toggle" onclick="return toggle('RDFS_OWLRL_Semantics');">-</a><tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-keyword">class</tt> <a class="py-def-name" href="RDFClosure.CombinedClosure.RDFS_OWLRL_Semantics-class.html">RDFS_OWLRL_Semantics</a><tt class="py-op">(</tt><tt class="py-base-class">RDFS_Semantics</tt><tt class="py-op">,</tt> <tt class="py-base-class">OWLRL_Semantics</tt><tt class="py-op">)</tt><tt class="py-op">:</tt> </tt>
</div><div id="RDFS_OWLRL_Semantics-collapsed" style="display:none;" pad="+++" indent="++++"></div><div id="RDFS_OWLRL_Semantics-expanded"><a name="L32"></a><tt class="py-lineno"> 32</tt>  <tt class="py-line">        <tt class="py-docstring">"""Common subclass of the RDFS and OWL 2 RL semantic classes. All methods simply call back</tt> </tt>
<a name="L33"></a><tt class="py-lineno"> 33</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring">        to the functions in the superclasses. This may lead to some unnecessary duplication of terms</tt> </tt>
<a name="L34"></a><tt class="py-lineno"> 34</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring">        and rules, but it it not so bad. Also, the additional identification defined for OWL Full,</tt> </tt>
<a name="L35"></a><tt class="py-lineno"> 35</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring">        ie, Resource being the same as Thing and OWL and RDFS classes being identical are added to the</tt> </tt>
<a name="L36"></a><tt class="py-lineno"> 36</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring">        triple store.</tt> </tt>
<a name="L37"></a><tt class="py-lineno"> 37</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring">        </tt> </tt>
<a name="L38"></a><tt class="py-lineno"> 38</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring">        Note that this class is also a possible user extension point: subclasses can be created that</tt> </tt>
<a name="L39"></a><tt class="py-lineno"> 39</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring">        extend the standard functionality by extending this class. This class I{always} performs RDFS inferences.</tt> </tt>
<a name="L40"></a><tt class="py-lineno"> 40</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring">        Subclasses have to set the C{self.rdfs} flag explicitly to the requested value if that is to be controlled.</tt> </tt>
<a name="L41"></a><tt class="py-lineno"> 41</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring">        </tt> </tt>

</dd></dl>

<hr />
<p>Common subclass of the RDFS and OWL 2 RL semantic classes. All methods
  simply call back to the functions in the superclasses. This may lead to 
  some unnecessary duplication of terms and rules, but it it not so bad. 
  Also, the additional identification defined for OWL Full, ie, Resource 
  being the same as Thing and OWL and RDFS classes being identical are 
  added to the triple store.</p>
  <p>Note that this class is also a possible user extension point: 
  subclasses can be created that extend the standard functionality by 
  extending this class. This class <i>always</i> performs RDFS inferences. 
  Subclasses have to set the <code>self.rdfs</code> flag explicitly to the 
  requested value if that is to be controlled.</p>

    </td>
  </tr></table>
  
  <p>If an extension wants to add new datatypes, this method should be 
  invoked at initialization time.</p>
  <dl class="fields">
    <dt>Parameters:</dt>
    <dd><ul class="nomargin-top">
        <li><strong class="pname"><code>uri</code></strong> - URI for the new datatypes, like owl_ns[&quot;Rational&quot;]</li>
        <li><strong class="pname"><code>conversion_function</code></strong> - a function converting the lexical representation of the datatype 
          to a Python value, possibly raising an exception in case of 
          unsuitable lexical form</li>
        <li><strong class="pname"><code>datatype_list</code></strong> - list of datatypes already in use that has to be checked</li>
        <li><strong class="pname"><code>subsumption_dict</code></strong> - dictionary of subsumption hierarchies (indexed by the datatype 
          URI-s)</li>
        <li><strong class="pname"><code>subsumption_key</code></strong> - key in the dictionary, if None, the uri parameter is used</li>
        <li><strong class="pname"><code>subsumption_list</code></strong> - list of subsumptions associated to a subsumption key (ie, all 
          datatypes that are superclasses of the new datatype)</li>
    </ul></dd>
  </dl>
</td></tr></table>
</div>

<!-- ==================== MODULE DESCRIPTION ==================== -->
<h1 class="epydoc">Module DatatypeHandling</h1><p class="nomargin-top"><span class="codelink"><a href="RDFClosure.DatatypeHandling-pysrc.html">source&nbsp;code</a></span></p>
<p>Most of the XSD datatypes are handled directly by RDFLib. However, in 
  some cases, that is not good enough. There are two major reasons for 
  this:</p>
  <ol start="1">
    <li>
      Some datatypes are missing from RDFLib and required by OWL 2 RL 
      and/or RDFS
    </li>
    <li>
      In other cases, though the datatype is present, RDFLib is fairly lax 
      in checking the lexical value of those datatypes. Typical case is 
      boolean.
    </li>
  </ol>
  <p>Some of these deficiencies are handled by this module. All the 
  functions convert the lexical value into a python datatype (or return the
  original string if this is not possible) which will be used, eg, for 
  comparisons (equalities). If the lexical value constraints are not met, 
  exceptions are raised.</p>

<hr />
<div class="fields">      <p><strong>Requires:</strong>
        <a href="https://github.com/RDFLib/rdflib" 
        target="_top">RDFLib</a>, 4.0.0 and higher
      </p>
      <p><strong>License:</strong>
        This software is available for use under the <a 
        href="http://www.w3.org/Consortium/Legal/2002/copyright-software-20021231"
        target="_top">W3C Software License</a>
      </p>
      <p><strong>Organization:</strong>
        <a href="http://www.w3.org" target="_top">World Wide Web 
        Consortium</a>
      </p>
      <p><strong>Author:</strong>
        <a href="http://ahref=&quot;http://www.w3.org/People/Ivan/&quot;" 
        target="_top">Ivan Herman</a>
      </p>
      <p><strong>Contact:</strong>
        Ivan Herman, ivan@w3.org
      </p>
</div><!-- ==================== CLASSES ==================== -->

<a name="_strToDecimal"></a>
<div class="private">
<table class="details" border="1" cellpadding="3"
       cellspacing="0" width="100%" bgcolor="white">
<tr><td>
  <table width="100%" cellpadding="0" cellspacing="0" border="0">
  <tr valign="top"><td>
  <h3 class="epydoc"><span class="sig"><span class="sig-name">_strToDecimal</span>(<span class="sig-arg">v</span>)</span>
  </h3>
  </td><td align="right" valign="top"
    ><span class="codelink"><a href="RDFClosure.DatatypeHandling-pysrc.html#_strToDecimal">source&nbsp;code</a></span>&nbsp;
    </td>
  </tr></table>
  
  <p>The built in datatype handling for RDFLib maps a decimal number to 
  float, but the python version 2.4 and upwards also has a Decimal number. 
  Better make use of that to use very high numbers. However, there is also 
  a big difference between Python's decimal and XSD's decimal, because the 
  latter does not allow for an exponential normal form (why???). This must 
  be filtered out.</p>
  <dl class="fields">
    <dt>Parameters:</dt>
    <dd><ul class="nomargin-top">
        <li><strong class="pname"><code>v</code></strong> - the literal string defined as decimal @return Decimal</li>
    </ul></dd>
    <dt>Raises:</dt>
    <dd><ul class="nomargin-top">
        <li><code><strong class='fraise'>ValueError</strong></code> - invalid decimal value</li>
    </ul></dd>
  </dl>
</td></tr></table>
</div>

<a name="_strToDouble"></a>
<div class="private">
<table class="details" border="1" cellpadding="3"
       cellspacing="0" width="100%" bgcolor="white">
<tr><td>
  <table width="100%" cellpadding="0" cellspacing="0" border="0">
  <tr valign="top"><td>
  <h3 class="epydoc"><span class="sig"><span class="sig-name">_strToDouble</span>(<span class="sig-arg">v</span>)</span>
  </h3>
  </td><td align="right" valign="top"
    ><span class="codelink"><a href="RDFClosure.DatatypeHandling-pysrc.html#_strToDouble">source&nbsp;code</a></span>&nbsp;
    </td>
  </tr></table>
  
  <p>Test and convert a double value into a Decimal or float. Raises an 
  exception if the number is outside the permitted range, ie, 1.0E+310 and 
  1.0E-330. To be on the safe side (python does not have double!) Decimals 
  are used if possible. Upper and lower values, as required by xsd, are 
  checked (and these fixed values are the reasons why Decimal is used!)</p>
  <dl class="fields">
    <dt>Parameters:</dt>
    <dd><ul class="nomargin-top">
        <li><strong class="pname"><code>v</code></strong> - the literal string defined as a double @return Decimal</li>
    </ul></dd>
    <dt>Raises:</dt>
    <dd><ul class="nomargin-top">
        <li><code><strong class='fraise'>ValueError</strong></code> - invalid value</li>
    </ul></dd>
  </dl>
</td></tr></table>
</div>

<a name="use_Alt_lexical_conversions"></a>
<div>
<table class="details" border="1" cellpadding="3"
       cellspacing="0" width="100%" bgcolor="white">
<tr><td>
  <table width="100%" cellpadding="0" cellspacing="0" border="0">
  <tr valign="top"><td>
  <h3 class="epydoc"><span class="sig"><span class="sig-name">use_Alt_lexical_conversions</span>()</span>
  </h3>
  </td><td align="right" valign="top"
    ><span class="codelink"><a href="RDFClosure.DatatypeHandling-pysrc.html#use_Alt_lexical_conversions">source&nbsp;code</a></span>&nbsp;
    </td>
  </tr></table>
  
  <p>Registering the datatypes item for RDFLib, ie, bind the dictionary 
  values. The 'bind' method of RDFLib adds extra datatypes to the 
  registered ones in RDFLib, though the table used here (ie, <a 
  href="RDFClosure.DatatypeHandling-module.html#AltXSDToPYTHON" 
  class="link">AltXSDToPYTHON</a>) actually overrides all of the default 
  conversion routines. The method also add a Decimal entry to the 
  PythonToXSD array of RDFLib.</p>
  <dl class="fields">
  </dl>
</td></tr></table>
</div>

<h1 class="epydoc">Source Code for <a href="RDFClosure.DatatypeHandling-module.html">Module RDFClosure.DatatypeHandling</a></h1>
<pre class="py-src">
<a name="L1"></a><tt class="py-lineno">  1</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-comment">#!/d/Bin/Python/python.exe</tt> </tt>
<a name="L2"></a><tt class="py-lineno">  2</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-comment"># -*- coding: utf-8 -*-</tt> </tt>
<a name="L3"></a><tt class="py-lineno">  3</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-comment">#</tt> </tt>
<a name="L4"></a><tt class="py-lineno">  4</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring">"""</tt> </tt>
<a name="L5"></a><tt class="py-lineno">  5</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring">Most of the XSD datatypes are handled directly by RDFLib. However, in some cases, that is not good enough. There are two</tt> </tt>
<a name="L6"></a><tt class="py-lineno">  6</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring">major reasons for this:</tt> </tt>
<a name="L7"></a><tt class="py-lineno">  7</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring"></tt> </tt>
<a name="L8"></a><tt class="py-lineno">  8</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring"> 1. Some datatypes are missing from RDFLib and required by OWL 2 RL and/or RDFS</tt> </tt>
<a name="L9"></a><tt class="py-lineno">  9</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring"> 2. In other cases, though the datatype is present, RDFLib is fairly lax in checking the lexical value of those datatypes. Typical case is boolean.</tt> </tt>
<a name="L10"></a><tt class="py-lineno"> 10</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring"></tt> </tt>
<a name="L11"></a><tt class="py-lineno"> 11</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring">Some of these deficiencies are handled by this module. All the functions convert the lexical value into a</tt> </tt>
<a name="L12"></a><tt class="py-lineno"> 12</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring">python datatype (or return the original string if this is not possible) which will be used, eg,</tt> </tt>
<a name="L13"></a><tt class="py-lineno"> 13</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring">for comparisons (equalities). If the lexical value constraints are not met, exceptions are raised.</tt> </tt>

<!-- ==================== CLASS DESCRIPTION ==================== -->
<h1 class="epydoc">Class _namelessTZ</h1><p class="nomargin-top"><span class="codelink"><a href="RDFClosure.DatatypeHandling-pysrc.html#_namelessTZ">source&nbsp;code</a></span></p>
<pre class="base-tree">
     object --+    
              |    
datetime.tzinfo --+
                  |
                 <strong class="uidshort">_namelessTZ</strong>
</pre>

<hr />
<p>(Nameless) timezone object. The python datetime object requires 
  timezones as a specific object added to the conversion, rather than the 
  explicit hour and minute difference used by XSD. This class is used to 
  wrap around the hour/minute values.</p>

<!-- ==================== CLASS DESCRIPTION ==================== -->
<h1 class="epydoc">Class DeductiveClosure</h1><p class="nomargin-top"><span class="codelink"><a href="RDFClosure-pysrc.html#DeductiveClosure">source&nbsp;code</a></span></p>
<p>Entry point to generate the deductive closure of a graph. The exact 
  choice deductive closure is controlled by a class reference. The 
  important initialization parameter is the <code>closure_class</code>: a 
  Class object referring to a subclass of <a 
  href="RDFClosure.Closure.Core-class.html" class="link">Closure.Core</a>. 
  Although this package includes a number of such subclasses (<a 
  href="RDFClosure.OWLRL.OWLRL_Semantics-class.html" 
  class="link">OWLRL_Semantics</a>, <a 
  href="RDFClosure.RDFSClosure.RDFS_Semantics-class.html" 
  class="link">RDFS_Semantics</a>, <a 
  href="RDFClosure.CombinedClosure.RDFS_OWLRL_Semantics-class.html" 
  class="link">RDFS_OWLRL_Semantics</a>, and <a 
  href="RDFClosure.OWLRLExtras.OWLRL_Extension-class.html" 
  class="link">OWLRL_Extension</a>), the user can use his/her own if 
  additional rules are implemented.</p>
  <p>Note that owl:imports statements are <i>not</i> interpreted in this 
  class, that has to be done beforehand on the graph that is to be 
  expanded.</p>

<!-- ==================== MODULE DESCRIPTION ==================== -->
<h1 class="epydoc">Module Literals</h1><p class="nomargin-top"><span class="codelink"><a href="RDFClosure.Literals-pysrc.html">source&nbsp;code</a></span></p>
<p>Separate module to handle literals.</p>
  <p>The issue is that pure literals cannot appear in subject position 
  according to the current rules on RDF. That means that different types of
  conclusions cannot properly finish. The present trick is trying to get 
  around the problem as follows:</p>
  <ol start="1">
    <li>
      For all literals in the graph a bnode is created. The module does not
      do a full D entailment but just relies on RDFLib's ability to 
      recognize identical literals
    </li>
    <li>
      All those bnodes get a type Literal
    </li>
    <li>
      All triples with literals are exchanged against a triple with the 
      associated bnode
    </li>
  </ol>
  <p>The inferences are then calculated with the modified Graph. At the end
  of the process, the above steps are done backwards: for all triples where
  a bnode representing a literal appear in object position, a triple is 
  generated; however, all triples where the bnode appears in a subject 
  position are removed from the final graph.</p>

<hr />
<div class="fields">      <p><strong>Requires:</strong>
        <a href="https://github.com/RDFLib/rdflib" 
        target="_top">RDFLib</a>, 4.0.0 and higher
      </p>
      <p><strong>License:</strong>
        This software is available for use under the <a 
        href="http://www.w3.org/Consortium/Legal/2002/copyright-software-20021231"
        target="_top">W3C Software License</a>
      </p>
      <p><strong>Organization:</strong>
        <a href="http://www.w3.org" target="_top">World Wide Web 
        Consortium</a>
      </p>
      <p><strong>Author:</strong>
        <a href="http://ahref=&quot;http://www.w3.org/People/Ivan/&quot;" 
        target="_top">Ivan Herman</a>
      </p>
      <p><strong>Contact:</strong>
        Ivan Herman, ivan@w3.org
      </p>

<a name="L13"></a><tt class="py-lineno"> 13</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring">The inferences are then calculated with the modified Graph. At the end of the process, the above steps are done backwards: for all triples where </tt> </tt>
<a name="L14"></a><tt class="py-lineno"> 14</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring">a bnode representing a literal appear in object position, a triple is generated; however, all triples where the bnode appears in a</tt> </tt>
<a name="L15"></a><tt class="py-lineno"> 15</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring">subject position are removed from the final graph.</tt> </tt>
<a name="L16"></a><tt class="py-lineno"> 16</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring"></tt> </tt>
<a name="L17"></a><tt class="py-lineno"> 17</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring"></tt> </tt>

<!-- ==================== CLASS DESCRIPTION ==================== -->
<h1 class="epydoc">Class _LiteralStructure</h1><p class="nomargin-top"><span class="codelink"><a href="RDFClosure.Literals-pysrc.html#_LiteralStructure">source&nbsp;code</a></span></p>
<p>This class serves as a wrapper around rdflib's Literal, by changing 
  the equality function to a strict identity of datatypes and lexical 
  values.</p>
  <p>On the other hand, to implement, eg, OWL RL's datatype rules, a should
  be able to generate an 'a sameAs b' triple, ie, the distinction should be
  kept. Hence this class that overrides the equality, and then can be used 
  as a key in a Python dictionary.</p>

<!-- ==================== MODULE DESCRIPTION ==================== -->
<h1 class="epydoc">Module OWL'</h1><p class="nomargin-top"><span class="codelink"><a href="RDFClosure.OWL%27-pysrc.html">source&nbsp;code</a></span></p>
<p>OWL and OWL2 terms. Note that the set of terms is <i>complete</i>, ie,
  it includes <i>all</i> OWL 2 terms, regardless of whether the term is 
  used in OWL 2 RL or not.</p>

<hr />
<div class="fields">      <p><strong>Requires:</strong>
        <a href="https://github.com/RDFLib/rdflib" 
        target="_top">RDFLib</a>, 4.0.0 and higher
      </p>

        This software is available for use under the <a 
        href="http://www.w3.org/Consortium/Legal/2002/copyright-software-20021231"
        target="_top">W3C Software License</a>
      </p>
      <p><strong>Organization:</strong>
        <a href="http://www.w3.org" target="_top">World Wide Web

      </p>
      <p><strong>Author:</strong>
        <a href="http://ahref=&quot;http://www.w3.org/People/Ivan/&quot;" 
        target="_top">Ivan Herman</a>
      </p>

<!-- ==================== MODULE DESCRIPTION ==================== -->
<h1 class="epydoc">Module OWLRL</h1><p class="nomargin-top"><span class="codelink"><a href="RDFClosure.OWLRL-pysrc.html">source&nbsp;code</a></span></p>
<p>This module is a <code>brute force</code> implementation of the OWL 2 
  RL profile.</p>
  <p>RDFLib works with 'generalized' RDF, meaning that triples with a BNode
  predicate are <i>allowed</i>. This is good because, eg, some of the 
  triples generated for RDF from an OWL 2 functional syntax might look like
  '[ owl:inverseOf p]', and the RL rules would then operate on such 
  generalized triple. However, as a last, post processing steps, these 
  triples are removed from the graph before serialization to produce 
  'standard' RDF (which is o.k. for RL, too, because the consequent triples
  are all right, generalized triples might have had a role in the deduction
  steps only).</p>

<hr />

        target="_top">RDFLib</a>, 4.0.0 and higher

<a name="L4"></a><tt class="py-lineno">  4</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring">"""</tt> </tt>
<a name="L5"></a><tt class="py-lineno">  5</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring">This module is a C{brute force} implementation of the OWL 2 RL profile.</tt> </tt>
<a name="L6"></a><tt class="py-lineno">  6</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring"></tt> </tt>
<a name="L7"></a><tt class="py-lineno">  7</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring">RDFLib works with 'generalized' RDF, meaning that triples with a BNode predicate are I{allowed}. This is good because, eg, some of the</tt> </tt>
<a name="L8"></a><tt class="py-lineno">  8</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring">triples generated for RDF from an OWL 2 functional syntax might look like '[ owl:inverseOf p]', and the RL rules would then operate</tt> </tt>
<a name="L9"></a><tt class="py-lineno">  9</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring">on such generalized triple. However, as a last, post processing steps, these triples are removed from the graph before serialization</tt> </tt>
<a name="L10"></a><tt class="py-lineno"> 10</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring">to produce 'standard' RDF (which is o.k. for RL, too, because the consequent triples are all right, generalized triples might</tt> </tt>
<a name="L11"></a><tt class="py-lineno"> 11</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring">have had a role in the deduction steps only).</tt> </tt>
<a name="L12"></a><tt class="py-lineno"> 12</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring"></tt> </tt>
<a name="L13"></a><tt class="py-lineno"> 13</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring">@requires: U{RDFLib&lt;https://github.com/RDFLib/rdflib&gt;}, 4.0.0 and higher</tt> </tt>
<a name="L14"></a><tt class="py-lineno"> 14</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring">@license: This software is available for use under the U{W3C Software License&lt;http://www.w3.org/Consortium/Legal/2002/copyright-software-20021231&gt;}</tt> </tt>

<!-- ==================== CLASS DESCRIPTION ==================== -->
<h1 class="epydoc">Class OWLRL_Semantics</h1><p class="nomargin-top"><span class="codelink"><a href="RDFClosure.OWLRL-pysrc.html#OWLRL_Semantics">source&nbsp;code</a></span></p>
<pre class="base-tree">
<a href="RDFClosure.Closure.Core-class.html">Closure.Core</a> --+
               |
              <strong class="uidshort">OWLRL_Semantics</strong>
</pre>

<dl><dt>Known Subclasses:</dt>
<dd>
      <ul class="subclass-list">
<li><a href="RDFClosure.CombinedClosure.RDFS_OWLRL_Semantics-class.html">CombinedClosure.RDFS_OWLRL_Semantics</a></li>  </ul>
</dd></dl>

<hr />
<p>OWL 2 RL Semantics class, ie, implementation of the OWL 2 RL closure 
  graph.</p>
  <p>Note that the module does <i>not</i> implement the so called Datatype 
  entailment rules, simply because the underlying RDFLib does not implement
  the datatypes (ie, RDFLib will not make the literal &quot;1.00&quot; and 
  &quot;1.00000&quot; identical, although even with all the ambiguities on 
  datatypes, this <i>should</i> be made equal...). Also, the so-called 
  extensional entailment rules (Section 7.3.1 in the RDF Semantics 
  document) have not been implemented either.</p>
  <p>The comments and references to the various rule follow the names as 
  used in the <a 
  href="http://www.w3.org/TR/owl2-profiles/#Reasoning_in_OWL_2_RL_and_RDF_Graphs_using_Rules"
  target="_top">OWL 2 RL document</a>.</p>

<a name="restriction_typing_check"></a>
<div>
<table class="details" border="1" cellpadding="3"
       cellspacing="0" width="100%" bgcolor="white">
<tr><td>
  <table width="100%" cellpadding="0" cellspacing="0" border="0">
  <tr valign="top"><td>
  <h3 class="epydoc"><span class="sig"><span class="sig-name">restriction_typing_check</span>(<span class="sig-arg">self</span>,
        <span class="sig-arg">v</span>,
        <span class="sig-arg">t</span>)</span>
  </h3>
  </td><td align="right" valign="top"
    ><span class="codelink"><a href="RDFClosure.OWLRL-pysrc.html#OWLRL_Semantics.restriction_typing_check">source&nbsp;code</a></span>&nbsp;
    </td>
  </tr></table>
  
  <p>Helping method to check whether a type statement is in line with a 
  possible restriction. This method is invoked by rule &quot;cls-avf&quot; 
  before setting a type on an allValuesFrom restriction.</p>
  <p>The method is a placeholder at this level. It is typically implemented
  by subclasses for extra checks, eg, for datatype facet checks.</p>
  <dl class="fields">
    <dt>Parameters:</dt>
    <dd><ul class="nomargin-top">
        <li><strong class="pname"><code>v</code></strong> - the resource that is to be 'typed'</li>
        <li><strong class="pname"><code>t</code></strong> - the targeted type (ie, Class)</li>
    </ul></dd>
    <dt>Returns:</dt>
        <dd>boolean</dd>
  </dl>
</td></tr></table>
</div>
<a name="_one_time_rules_datatypes"></a>
<div class="private">
<table class="details" border="1" cellpadding="3"
       cellspacing="0" width="100%" bgcolor="white">
<tr><td>
  <table width="100%" cellpadding="0" cellspacing="0" border="0">
  <tr valign="top"><td>
  <h3 class="epydoc"><span class="sig"><span class="sig-name">_one_time_rules_datatypes</span>(<span class="sig-arg">self</span>)</span>
  </h3>
  </td><td align="right" valign="top"
    ><span class="codelink"><a href="RDFClosure.OWLRL-pysrc.html#OWLRL_Semantics._one_time_rules_datatypes">source&nbsp;code</a></span>&nbsp;
    </td>
  </tr></table>
  
  <p>Some of the rules in the rule set are axiomatic in nature, meaning 
  that they really have to be added only once, there is no reason to add 
  these in a cycle. These are performed by this method that is invoked only
  once at the beginning of the process.</p>
  <p>These are: cls-thing, cls-nothing1, prp-ap, dt-types1, dt-types2, 
  dt-eq, dt-diff.</p>
  <p>Note, however, that the dt-* are executed only partially, limited by 
  the possibilities offered by RDFLib. These may not cover all the edge 
  cases of OWL RL. Especially, dt-not-type has not (yet?) been implemented 
  (I wonder whether RDFLib should not raise exception for those 
  anyway...</p>
  <dl class="fields">
  </dl>
</td></tr></table>
</div>
<a name="one_time_rules"></a>
<div>
<table class="details" border="1" cellpadding="3"
       cellspacing="0" width="100%" bgcolor="white">
<tr><td>
  <table width="100%" cellpadding="0" cellspacing="0" border="0">
  <tr valign="top"><td>
  <h3 class="epydoc"><span class="sig"><span class="sig-name">one_time_rules</span>(<span class="sig-arg">self</span>)</span>
  </h3>
  </td><td align="right" valign="top"
    ><span class="codelink"><a href="RDFClosure.OWLRL-pysrc.html#OWLRL_Semantics.one_time_rules">source&nbsp;code</a></span>&nbsp;
    </td>
  </tr></table>
  
  <p>Some of the rules in the rule set are axiomatic in nature, meaning 
  that they really have to be added only once, there is no reason to add 
  these in a cycle. These are performed by this method that is invoked only
  once at the beginning of the process.</p>
  <p>These are: cls-thing, cls-nothing1, prp-ap, dt-types1, dt-types2, 
  dt-eq, dt-diff.</p>
  <dl class="fields">
    <dt>Overrides:
        <a href="RDFClosure.Closure.Core-class.html#one_time_rules">Closure.Core.one_time_rules</a>
    </dt>
  </dl>
</td></tr></table>
</div>
<a name="rules"></a>
<div>
<table class="details" border="1" cellpadding="3"
       cellspacing="0" width="100%" bgcolor="white">
<tr><td>
  <table width="100%" cellpadding="0" cellspacing="0" border="0">
  <tr valign="top"><td>
  <h3 class="epydoc"><span class="sig"><span class="sig-name">rules</span>(<span class="sig-arg">self</span>,
        <span class="sig-arg">t</span>,
        <span class="sig-arg">cycle_num</span>)</span>
  </h3>
  </td><td align="right" valign="top"
    ><span class="codelink"><a href="RDFClosure.OWLRL-pysrc.html#OWLRL_Semantics.rules">source&nbsp;code</a></span>&nbsp;
    </td>
  </tr></table>
  
  <p>Go through the various rule groups, as defined in the OWL-RL profile 
  text and implemented via local methods. (The calling cycle takes every 
  tuple in the graph.)</p>
  <dl class="fields">
    <dt>Parameters:</dt>
    <dd><ul class="nomargin-top">
        <li><strong class="pname"><code>t</code></strong> - a triple (in the form of a tuple)</li>
        <li><strong class="pname"><code>cycle_num</code></strong> - which cycle are we in, starting with 1. This value is forwarded 
          to all local rules; it is also used locally to collect the bnodes
          in the graph.</li>
    </ul></dd>
    <dt>Overrides:
        <a href="RDFClosure.Closure.Core-class.html#rules">Closure.Core.rules</a>
    </dt>
  </dl>
</td></tr></table>
</div>

<!-- ==================== MODULE DESCRIPTION ==================== -->
<h1 class="epydoc">Module OWLRLExtras</h1><p class="nomargin-top"><span class="codelink"><a href="RDFClosure.OWLRLExtras-pysrc.html">source&nbsp;code</a></span></p>
<p>Extension to OWL 2 RL, ie, some additional rules added to the system 
  from OWL 2 Full. It is implemented through the <a 
  href="RDFClosure.OWLRLExtras.OWLRL_Extension-class.html" 
  class="link">OWLRL_Extension</a> class, whose reference has to be passed 
  to the relevant semantic class (ie, either the OWL 2 RL or the combined 
  closure class) as an 'extension'.</p>
  <p>The added rules and features are:</p>
  <ul>
    <li>
      self restriction
    </li>
    <li>
      owl:rational datatype
    </li>
    <li>
      datatype restrictions via facets
    </li>
  </ul>
  <p>In more details, the rules that are added:</p>
  <ol start="1">
    <li>
      self restriction 1: <code>?z owl:hasSelf ?x. ?x owl:onProperty ?p. ?y
      rdf:type ?z. =&gt; ?y ?p ?y.</code>
    </li>
    <li>
      self restriction 2: <code>?z owl:hasSelf ?x. ?x owl:onProperty ?p. ?y
      ?p ?y. =&gt; ?y rdf:type ?z. </code>
    </li>
  </ol>

<hr />
<div class="fields">      <p><strong>Requires:</strong>
        <a href="https://github.com/RDFLib/rdflib" 
        target="_top">RDFLib</a>, 4.0.0 and higher
      </p>

        This software is available for use under the <a 
        href="http://www.w3.org/Consortium/Legal/2002/copyright-software-20021231"
        target="_top">W3C Software License</a>
      </p>

        target="_top">Ivan Herman</a>
      </p>
      <p><strong>Contact:</strong>
        Ivan Herman, ivan@w3.org
      </p>

<a name="_strToRational"></a>
<div class="private">
<table class="details" border="1" cellpadding="3"
       cellspacing="0" width="100%" bgcolor="white">
<tr><td>
  <table width="100%" cellpadding="0" cellspacing="0" border="0">
  <tr valign="top"><td>
  <h3 class="epydoc"><span class="sig"><span class="sig-name">_strToRational</span>(<span class="sig-arg">v</span>)</span>
  </h3>
  </td><td align="right" valign="top"
    ><span class="codelink"><a href="RDFClosure.OWLRLExtras-pysrc.html#_strToRational">source&nbsp;code</a></span>&nbsp;
    </td>
  </tr></table>
  
  <p>Converting a string to a rational.</p>
  <p>According to the OWL spec: numerator must be an integer, denominator a
  positive integer (ie, xsd['integer'] type), and the denominator should 
  not have a '+' sign.</p>
  <dl class="fields">
    <dt>Parameters:</dt>
    <dd><ul class="nomargin-top">
        <li><strong class="pname"><code>v</code></strong> - the literal string defined as boolean @return corresponding 
          Rational value</li>
    </ul></dd>
    <dt>Returns: Rational</dt>
    <dt>Raises:</dt>
    <dd><ul class="nomargin-top">
        <li><code><strong class='fraise'>ValueError</strong></code> - invalid rational string literal</li>
    </ul></dd>
  </dl>
</td></tr></table>
</div>
<br />

<a name="L5"></a><tt class="py-lineno">  5</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring"></tt> </tt>
<a name="L6"></a><tt class="py-lineno">  6</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring">Extension to OWL 2 RL, ie, some additional rules added to the system from OWL 2 Full. It is implemented through</tt> </tt>
<a name="L7"></a><tt class="py-lineno">  7</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring">the L{OWLRL_Extension} class, whose reference has to be passed to the relevant semantic class (ie, either the OWL 2 RL or the combined</tt> </tt>
<a name="L8"></a><tt class="py-lineno">  8</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring">closure class) as an 'extension'.</tt> </tt>
<a name="L9"></a><tt class="py-lineno">  9</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring"></tt> </tt>
<a name="L10"></a><tt class="py-lineno"> 10</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring">The added rules and features are:</tt> </tt>
<a name="L11"></a><tt class="py-lineno"> 11</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring"></tt> </tt>
<a name="L12"></a><tt class="py-lineno"> 12</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring"> - self restriction</tt> </tt>
<a name="L13"></a><tt class="py-lineno"> 13</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring"> - owl:rational datatype</tt> </tt>
<a name="L14"></a><tt class="py-lineno"> 14</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring"> - datatype restrictions via facets</tt> </tt>
<a name="L15"></a><tt class="py-lineno"> 15</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring"> </tt> </tt>
<a name="L16"></a><tt class="py-lineno"> 16</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring">In more details, the rules that are added:</tt> </tt>
<a name="L17"></a><tt class="py-lineno"> 17</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring"></tt> </tt>
<a name="L18"></a><tt class="py-lineno"> 18</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring"> 1. self restriction 1: C{?z owl:hasSelf ?x. ?x owl:onProperty ?p. ?y rdf:type ?z. =&gt; ?y ?p ?y.}</tt> </tt>
<a name="L19"></a><tt class="py-lineno"> 19</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring"> 2. self restriction 2: C{?z owl:hasSelf ?x. ?x owl:onProperty ?p. ?y ?p ?y. =&gt; ?y rdf:type ?z. }</tt> </tt>
<a name="L20"></a><tt class="py-lineno"> 20</tt>  <tt class="py-line"><tt class="py-docstring"></tt> </tt>
